indicative noun and adjective

the mood

also indicative mood, in the indicative

late Latin

Diom. p. 329; Prisc. p. 819 P. (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 225, 247
Traupman 332

indicātīvus, indicātīva, indicātīvum

declension

indicative; as a noun (modus understood), the indicative

The later grammarians’ term, and every grammar’s since: modō indicātīvō, in the indicative mood (Traupman 247). Varro and Quintilian call it fatendī modus, “the mood of stating” (see below).

Other words

  • fatendī modus — the indicative, “the mood of stating”

    also used · classical · Quint. 1.6.7: quae e et o litterīs fatendī modō terminantur; Varr. LL 8.5.8 (Lewis & Short s.v. fateor)

    Varro’s and Quintilian’s name: the mood in which one declares or owns a thing (fatērī). The older name; the grammars and the classroom use the later one.

Examples

  • omnia, quae e et o litterīs fatendī modō terminantur, eadem, sī īnfīnītīs e litteram mediā syllabā accēpērunt, utique prōductam habent

    all verbs that end in e and o in the indicative have that e long, if they keep it in the middle syllable of the infinitiveQuint. 1.6.7

  • modō indicātīvō

    in the indicative moodTraupman 332

See also mood, subjunctive, imperative, grammar.

SourcesLewis & Short: fateor · Lewis & Short: indicativus
